Connectors endpoint v2

Manage connectors — the source and destination integrations pipelines read from and write to.

Create a connector

POST /v2/connectors

Name Type Required Description

Transforms endpoint v2

Create and manage transform steps that modify events as they flow through a pipeline. Base URL: https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2.

Create a transform

POST /v2/transforms

Name Type Required Description
pipeline_idstringYesID of the pipeline this transform step belongs to.
namestringYesHuman-readable transform name, unique within the pipeline.
typestringYesOne of filter, map, enrich, or aggregate.
configobjectYesType-specific configuration, e.g. filter expression or mapping rules.
positionintegerNoOrder within the pipeline's transform sequence (0-indexed). Defaults to end of sequence.
create-transform.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/transforms \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "pipeline_id": "pl_ingest_orders",
    "name": "filter-high-value",
    "type": "filter",
    "config": { "expression": "amount > 1000" }
  }'

List transforms

GET /v2/transforms?pipeline_id={pipeline_id} — returns all transform steps for a pipeline, ordered by their position in the sequence.

list-transforms.sh bash 
curl https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/transforms?pipeline_id=pl_ingest_orders \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"

Transform types

Each transform type accepts a different config object shape:

  • filter — expression string with a boolean condition that determines which events pass through.
  • map — rules object mapping source fields to destination fields or computed values.
  • enrich — source connector ID and lookup_field for joining external data.
  • aggregate — group_by fields and aggregations array defining the output schema.
Transform order matters

Transforms are applied in sequence based on their position. A filter applied before a map sees the original event structure; the same filter after the map sees the mapped fields.

Webhooks endpoint v2

Subscribe to platform lifecycle events — such as pipeline.completed or connector.error — as outbound HTTP requests to a URL you control. This is the v2 replacement for v1's polling-only status checks; see the Migration guide if you're moving off v1.

Create a webhook subscription

POST /v2/webhooks

Name Type Required Description
urlstringYesHTTPS endpoint Godzilla will POST events to.
eventsarrayYesList of event types to subscribe to, e.g. [\"pipeline.failed\"].
secretstringNoShared secret used to sign the X-Godzilla-Signature header. Auto-generated if omitted.
webhook-payload.json json 
{
  "id": "evt_wh_2091",
  "type": "pipeline.failed",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:14:02Z",
  "data": { "pipeline_id": "pl_ingest_orders", "error": "destination_timeout" }
}
Verify the signature

Always verify X-Godzilla-Signature before trusting a webhook payload. Unsigned or unverifiable requests to your endpoint should be rejected, not processed.

Delivery retries

A webhook delivery that doesn't receive a 2xx response is retried with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours, then marked failed. Failed deliveries are visible per-subscription and can be manually redelivered.

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Handling errors & retries

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

pipeline-retry-config.json json 
{
  "retry_policy": {
    "max_attempts": 5,
    "backoff": "exponential",
    "initial_delay_ms": 1000
  }
}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

schedule.json json 
{
  "schedule": "0 */4 * * *"
}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

Choosing between them

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Handling errors & retries.

Transforming events in flight

This guide covers how to reshape, filter, and enrich events as they pass through a pipeline — transforming raw data from your source into the exact shape your destination expects.

Reshaping event structure

A transform extracts fields from the incoming event and maps them to a new output structure. Use transforms to flatten nested data, rename fields, or select only the columns you need.

reshape-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "jmespath",
    "expression": "{ id: user.id, email: user.contact.email, created: timestamp }"
  }
}

Filtering events

Filter out events that don't meet your criteria — for example, dropping test transactions or skipping events from staging environments. Filtered events are still recorded in the pipeline's audit log but do not reach your destination.

filter-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "filter",
    "condition": "environment == 'production' && amount > 100"
  }
}
Filtered events are not lost

Filtered events skip the destination write but remain queryable in your pipeline's event history. Use the API to review what was filtered and when.

Enriching events

Add computed fields, lookups from external systems, or metadata to each event before it reaches your destination. Enrichments can call out to external APIs, query a database, or perform calculations on the event data.

enrich-transform.json json 
{
  "transform": {
    "type": "enrich",
    "lookup": {
      "service": "user-api",
      "key_field": "user_id",
      "output_fields": ["tier", "region", "last_login"]
    }
  }
}

Chaining multiple transforms

Transforms run in sequence — the output of one becomes the input to the next. This lets you filter first, reshape second, and enrich last, keeping your logic modular and testable.

Transform performance

Enrichments that call external services add latency. Consider caching results, using batch lookups, or pre-computing enrichments upstream of your pipeline if throughput is critical.

Testing transforms locally

Use the Pipelines endpoint to dry-run a transform against sample events before deploying it to production. This lets you validate your JMESPath expressions and filter conditions without risking live data.

Next steps

With your events shaped correctly, see Handling errors & retries to understand what happens when a transformed event fails to reach your destination.

Backfill historical data

When you set up a new pipeline, you often want to load historical data that already exists in your source system. This recipe shows how to configure your pipeline to replay data from the past without disrupting real-time event flow.

The pattern

Backfilling typically involves two phases:

  1. Batch load: Query your source system for all historical records within a date range.
  2. Stream events: Once historical data catches up, switch to real-time event streaming for ongoing updates.

Godzilla pipelines support both approaches through the same connectors and destination configuration, so you can use one pipeline for both historical and real-time data.

Set up a source connector with a date filter

Most source connectors accept configuration options to limit which records to pull. For example, a Postgres source can query records after a specific timestamp:

backfill-source.json json 
{
  "type": "postgres",
  "direction": "source",
  "config": {
    "connection_string": "postgres://user:pass@host/db",
    "query": "SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01'",
    "polling_interval_seconds": 3600
  }
}

The polling_interval_seconds setting controls how often the source checks for new records. For backfill, you might use a longer interval (like 3600 seconds = 1 hour) to avoid overwhelming your source system.

Create the pipeline

Your backfill pipeline works exactly like any other pipeline. Create it using the source connector from the previous step and your destination:

create-backfill-pipeline.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "backfill-events",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_pg_backfill",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_dw"
  }'

Monitor backfill progress

Use the Pipelines endpoint to check how many events have been processed:

check-progress.sh bash 
curl -X GET https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines/backfill-events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"

The response includes stats.events_processed and stats.events_failed so you can track progress in real time. See Monitoring & alerts to set up notifications when backfill completes.

Next steps

Once your historical data is loaded, you can create a second real-time pipeline using the same destination but with a source connector configured to stream only new events (from the current moment forward).

Fan-out to multiple destinations

In real-world data architectures, you often need to send the same event stream to multiple destination systems — a data warehouse for analytics, a search index for product search, a real-time API for notifications, and so on. This recipe shows how to fan out a single pipeline's output across several destinations.

The pattern

Each Godzilla pipeline has one source and one destination. To fan out to multiple destinations, create one pipeline per destination, all reading from the same source connector:

fanout-pattern.txt text 
Source (Kafka topic)
  ├─ Pipeline A ──> Snowflake (analytics)
  ├─ Pipeline B ──> Elasticsearch (search)
  └─ Pipeline C ──> DynamoDB (real-time API)

All three pipelines read the same events in the same order, but transform and deliver them to their respective destinations independently.

Set up a shared source connector

First, create a single source connector for the data you want to fan out. This example uses a Kafka topic:

create-kafka-source.sh bash 
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "type": "kafka",
    "direction": "source",
    "config": {
      "bootstrap_servers": "kafka.example.com:9092",
      "topic": "user-events",
      "consumer_group": "godzilla-fan-out"
    }
  }'

Store the returned connector_id (e.g., conn_kafka_users) — you'll use it for all downstream pipelines.

Create destination connectors

Next, create one destination connector for each system you're fanning out to:

create-destinations.sh bash 
# Snowflake for analytics
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "type": "snowflake",
    "direction": "destination",
    "config": {"account": "xy12345.us-east-1", "warehouse": "COMPUTE_WH"}
  }'

# Elasticsearch for search
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "type": "elasticsearch",
    "direction": "destination",
    "config": {"hosts": ["elastic.example.com:9200"]}
  }'

# DynamoDB for real-time API
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "type": "dynamodb",
    "direction": "destination",
    "config": {"table_name": "user-events", "region": "us-east-1"}
  }'

Create one pipeline per destination

Now create a pipeline for each destination, all using the same source connector:

create-fanout-pipelines.sh bash 
# Pipeline to Snowflake
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "user-events-to-snowflake",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_users",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_snowflake_analytics"
  }'

# Pipeline to Elasticsearch
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "user-events-to-elasticsearch",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_users",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_elasticsearch_search"
  }'

# Pipeline to DynamoDB
curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "name": "user-events-to-dynamodb",
    "source_connector_id": "conn_kafka_users",
    "destination_connector_id": "conn_dynamodb_api"
  }'

Transform events per destination

Each pipeline can apply different transformations before writing to its destination. For example, reshape data for Elasticsearch's flat schema, or extract only the fields DynamoDB needs:

transformation-example.json json 
{
  "type": "jq",
  "expr": "{ id: .user_id, name: .user_name, email: .user_email, updated_at: now }"
}

Monitor all pipelines

Each pipeline has independent monitoring and alerts. Use the Pipelines endpoint to check the health of each fan-out branch. See Monitoring & alerts for setting up per-pipeline notifications.

Ordering and delivery

All three pipelines will receive events in the same order (because they read from the same Kafka partition group), but they may write to their destinations at slightly different rates depending on network latency and destination throughput. If your use case requires strict ordering across all destinations, use a single pipeline with a custom transformation that writes to all three systems in a transaction, or consider using a message queue pattern instead.
